function.name: read
function.description: Read a file from the workspace. Output is line-numbered, so you can quote exact lines back when editing. Reads the whole file by default; use offset and limit for a range of a large file. You must read a file before editing or overwriting it.

path.description: Path to the file, absolute or relative to the working directory.

offset.description: First line to return, 1-based. Omit to start at the beginning.

limit.description: How many lines to return. Omit for the default window.

function.name: write
function.description: Create a new file, or replace an existing one entirely. Read an existing file before overwriting it. Prefer edit for changing part of a file: rewriting a whole file to change three lines loses everything you did not remember to keep.

path.description: Path to write, absolute or relative to the working directory.

content.description: The complete new contents of the file.

function.name: edit
function.description: Replace an exact string in a file you have already read. The old string must appear exactly once unless replace_all is set, so include enough surrounding lines to make it unique. Strip the line-number prefix that read adds before matching.

old_string.description: Exact text to replace, including indentation.

new_string.description: Replacement text. Must differ from old_string.

replace_all.description: Replace every occurrence instead of requiring exactly one. Use for renames.

function.name: apply_patch

patch.description: The whole patch, from `*** Begin Patch` to `*** End Patch`.

function.name: glob
function.description: Find files by name pattern, e.g. `**/*.rs` or `src/**/test_*.py`. Files git ignores are skipped by default. Results are sorted by path. Use this to locate files; use grep to search inside them.

pattern.description: Glob pattern matched against the path relative to the search root.

path.description: Directory to search. Defaults to the working directory.

include_ignored.description: Include files listed in .gitignore. Off by default.

function.name: grep
function.description: Search file contents with a regular expression (Rust regex syntax). Files git ignores and binary files are skipped. Use output_mode `files` when you only need to know where something lives, and `content` when you need to read the matching lines.

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the working directory.

glob.description: Only search files matching this glob, e.g. `**/*.rs`.

output_mode.description: What to return. Defaults to content.

function.name: bash
function.description:
Run a shell command in the workspace. Use it for builds, tests, git, and anything else with no dedicated tool. Prefer read, glob, and grep for looking at files: they are faster and their output is easier to work with. Quote paths that contain spaces.

Set `run_in_background` for something with no end — a dev server, a watcher — and read it later with `job`.

description.description: One short sentence describing what this does, shown to the user when they are asked to approve it.

timeout_secs.description: How long to wait before killing the command. Defaults to 120.

run_in_background.description: Start it and leave it running instead of waiting. For dev servers, watchers and anything else with no end: use `job` to read its output, and `job kill` to stop it. Not for slow commands you need the result of — raise timeout_secs for those.

function.name: todo_write
function.description: Record the plan for a multi-step task, and update it as you go. Send the whole list every time — it replaces the previous one. Keep exactly one item in_progress: a plan where everything is in progress says nothing about where you are. Mark an item completed as soon as it is done rather than in a batch at the end, so someone reading along knows what is left. Skip it entirely for work that is one or two obvious steps.

todos.description: The complete list, replacing whatever was there.

content.description: What has to be done, as an instruction.

active_form.description: The same thing in present tense, shown while it is the item being worked on.

function.name: goal_done
function.description: Declare the standing goal complete. Only when a goal is set, and only once the whole of it is done and verified — not when one step is. Until you call this the harness keeps asking you to continue, so calling it is how the work ends. The summary is for the person who set the goal: what was done, what was checked, and anything they should look at.

summary.description: What was done and how it was verified, in a few sentences.

function.name: job
function.description:
Look in on commands started with `run_in_background`.

`list` — everything this session started, and whether it is still up.
`read` — whatever one has written since you last read it. Reading twice in a row returns nothing the second time, so poll it rather than re-reading from the start.
`kill` — stop one. Do this when you are finished with a server you started; it will otherwise hold its port until the session ends.

job.description: Which job, as returned when it was started. Required for read and kill.

function.name: skill
function.description: Load the written-down instructions for a kind of work. Call this at the start of a task that matches one of them, before planning and before reading the code — the instructions are mostly about how to begin, so loading one afterwards recovers little of what it was for. The system prompt lists each skill and when it applies. Available: investigate, fix-a-failing-test, review-your-changes, write-a-commit, review-code, write-tests, debug, refactor-safely, resolve-conflicts, review-frontend, review-security, test-a-web-app, write-a-skill, write-project-notes, make-a-deck, make-a-document, make-a-spreadsheet, work-with-pdfs, research.

The bug is in `_batched_insert` at line 1212:
```python
batch_size = (batch_size or max(ops.bulk_batch_size(fields, objs), 1))
```

This line means:
- If `batch_size` is provided (truthy), use it as-is.
- If `batch_size` is None, use `max(ops.bulk_batch_size(fields, objs), 1)`.

The problem: when a user provides a `batch_size` that is **larger** than the backend's maximum allowed batch size (`ops.bulk_batch_size`), the user's value is used directly, which can exceed the backend's limit. This can cause errors on backends like SQLite (999 variables per query) or Oracle.

```python
max_batch_size = connections[self.db].ops.bulk_batch_size(['pk', 'pk'] + fields, objs)
batch_size = min(batch_size, max_batch_size) if batch_size else max_batch_size
```

This correctly takes the minimum of the user-provided `batch_size` and the backend's `max_batch_size`.
